transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-14
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 1h18m (78 minutes)
Attendees: Jamal Rivera (Redwood AE), Priya Malhotra (Redwood SE), Omar Li (Redwood Perf Eng), Elena Vos (Strata Head of ML Platform), Marco Reyes (Strata Infra), Tara Shin (Strata MLOps)

Summary: Short recap at top - Redwood team walked through nonlinear slicing approach for ultra-long prompts (128k+), a multi-tier KV hierarchy to keep hot prefixes in fast GPU memory and colder context in remote SSD-backed KV. Discussed latency SLOs (p95/p99), batching policies, async prefetching, and VPC constraints for private deployment.

--- Action items mentioned in call: see metadata list above.

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, automated transcription with some errors):
[00:00] Jamal: All right, hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. we're gonna jump into a deep dive, Priya and Omar will run through the nonlinear slicing idea and then we can map that to Strata's infra.
[00:18] Elena: Thanks Jamal, yeah excited. We've been seeing model runs that need 150k tokens internal docs + user history, so we need a clear path for p99 under 700ms if possible, but cost is also a big constraint.
[00:32] Priya: Cool. quick note: when I say "nonlinear slicing" i'm referring to chunking that isn't fixed-size append; we prioritize semantic boundaries and use a variable-size windowing so the runtime can drop irrelevant middle spans faster, the idea is to reduce effective attention cost while preserving important long-range references.
[00:50] Marco: sorry, can you rephrase "drop middle spans" — do you mean evicting from KV or not sending them to attention at all?
[00:57] Priya: Good call. There are two levels — one is not materializing that span into GPU attention for the current token (so no KV load), and second is eviction from the in-GPU KV cache to a lower tier. so both.
[01:12] Tara: That makes sense, but our infra team is worried about consistency — e.g., when we evict a span, do we lose determinism for evaluation requests?
[01:22] Omar: We actually ran A/B tests — small chance of nondeterminism exists because of async prefetch ordering, but for production you can pin model version + adopt a strict fallback policy: if relevant context isn't found, fallback to smaller window deterministic pass. Tradeoff is latency.
[01:38] Elena: Can you quantify — what latency penalty on fallback?
[01:42] Priya: If we miss and have to run a second pass, that's roughly an extra 80-140ms on top of base, depends on batch size and sequence lengths. with 128k workloads, worst-case 250ms extra for a full cold pipeline in our tests.
[01:56] Marco: what's base p99 we should expect on dedicated 8x A100s with Redwood runtime?
[02:02] Omar: For a 1-2 concurrent streams at 128k, with KV hot set in GPU and async prefetch tuned, p99 was around 420-520ms in lab; but that assumes prefix caching and continuous batching. If your hot set is smaller, numbers improve.
[02:17] Elena: What's continuous batching here?
[02:21] Priya: Redwood's continuous batching pools micro-requests across a sliding window and emits a single GPU batch when filling heuristics are met — reduces per-token cost. For long context we adapt heuristics to prefer lower latency by reducing allowed wait time; it's a knob you can tune per route.
[02:39] Marco: Are there risks with continuous batching in a VPC/on-prem network environment? we have variable egress latency to the control plane.
[02:47] Omar: Good question — control-plane variability doesn't affect the runtime's local batching loop because serving nodes coordinate over a local RPC at the rack layer. However, if you use a private control plane with VPC peering, we recommend colocating cache nodes to minimize cross-subnet jitter.
[03:05] Tara: you mentioned hierarchical KV earlier — can you walk the tiers?
[03:09] Priya: Sure — tier 0 is in-GPU KV (fastest, limited by GPU memory), tier 1 is host-DRAM backed per-node cache with async eviction, tier 2 is remote SSD/filestore with an index (we call it cold store). Lookups prefer tier 0 then 1 then 2. We also have bloom-filter style membership checks to avoid fetching full objects unnecessarily.
[03:30] Marco: And indexing for 128k windows — are keys per chunk or per sentence?
[03:35] Priya: We generally key per semantic chunk (variable length) with boundary tokens stored. For indexing we use a compact fingerprint; it reduces KV object count and improves eviction locality.
[03:46] Elena: How does quantization affect KV entries, e.g., if model weights are 4-bit/8-bit — do you keep KV in quantized form?
[03:54] Omar: We experimented with quantized KV. For int8/4-bit we saw ~12-28% memory saving on KV without large degradation in retrieval quality for most tasks. But quantization noise can amplify in long chains — for some instruction-following tasks we saw subtle hallucination increases. So default is to keep KV in fp16 in GPU and allow quantized cold tiers.
[04:14] Marco: So cold tiers on SSD can be quantized to 4-bit?
[04:16] Priya: Yes, that's the usual pattern. decompress on load to host DRAM then do a fast dequantize path into GPU if needed.
[04:23] [05:00] Elena: Network and storage IO look like the biggest unknowns for us. We are on AWS in a VPC with strict egress policies. How would Redwood run benchmark tests inside our VPC?
[05:12] Jamal: Typically we ask for time-limited cross-account role + S3/VPC peering for data pulls; for deeper tests Redwood provides a private deployment bundle (image + helm charts) that you can deploy inside your VPC. We can also run with a remote perf agent if peering is not allowed but results are noisier.
[05:28] Marco: We prefer the image inside our VPC. Are there additional networking requirements?
[05:33] Omar: Minimal — control-plane calls for metrics and rollouts can be configured to use a private endpoint. Serving traffic stays internal once set up. Also recommend dedicating EBS throughput for cold-store SSDs to avoid IO spikes.
[05:46] Tara: about benchmarks — what metrics should we collect to compare strategies?
[05:50] Priya: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec throughput, percent of requests that hit tier0, percent cold fetches, extra fallback rate, cost per 1M tokens (estimated), and model output quality deltas on a held-out eval set. Also collect end-to-end tail CPU usage on the host.
[06:10] Elena: That sounds right. can you share a minimal harness we can run?
[06:13] Priya: Yes we'll share a harness that has a synthetic long-context generator to mimic your docs plus a real sample corpus you send. It supports toggling quantization, batch window, async prefetch depth, and eviction thresholds.
[06:24] Marco: If we want deterministic evaluation, is it ok to disable async prefetch and batching?
[06:28] Omar: You can disable both and get deterministic runs but you pay in latency and cost. We usually run deterministic baseline then enable production knobs and measure variance.
[06:37] [10:05] Marco: on the topic of chunking algorithm, are you using any learned selectors to choose which spans to materialize?
[10:11] Priya: Yes — we prototype a lightweight selector model that scores spans by relevance using compressed representations. It's trained on pairwise relevance in your domain. For production we often use a hybrid: fast heuristic (TF-IDF+sentencenc) plus the learned selector as a second pass for ambiguous cases.
[10:28] Tara: That seems heavy. what's the latency cost for running the selector?
[10:31] Priya: The fast heuristic runs in ~4-6ms per chunk on host CPU, the learned selector is ~12-20ms but can be batched and run async. We avoid running it synchronously in the critical path whenever possible.
[10:45] Elena: Any memory/compute cost for maintaining chunk metadata at 150k tokens?
[10:51] Omar: Metadata is tiny; think fingerprints and offsets. for 150k effective tokens we saw ~150-400KB of metadata per document depending on chunk granularity. Not a big driver; KV vector objects are the main memory consumer.
[11:06] [18:00] Elena: I want to call out compliance — we need SOC2 and KMS integration. If we run the private image in our VPC how does Redwood support KMS/HSM?
[18:12] Jamal: We support customer-managed KMS for keys used by the control plane and optional integration with HSM for keystore. The private bundle can be configured to use your KMS; audit logs can be forwarded to your S3/Audit endpoint.
[18:30] Marco: And for RBAC / SSO?
[18:33] Priya: Support for SAML/SSO, fine-grained RBAC integrated with your IdP. In on-prem we can map roles to Kubernetes RBAC.
[18:42] Tara: Good. Back to performance — how do you handle KV eviction policies for long lived sessions? we sometimes have very long user histories that we can't drop.
[18:52] Omar: We implement a recency-frequency hybrid with semantic aging — spans that are semantically less relevant get a lower score and are evicted earlier. You can also pin spans for a session if you know they must persist. Pinning consumes tier0 capacity but guarantees availability.
[19:10] Marco: Is pinning per session or global?
[19:13] Priya: Per session by default, with options for cross-session sticky pins.
[19:18] [24:30] Elena: For quantization, I'm worried about rare-case hallucinations. any guardrails?
[24:35] Omar: Yes, two layers — first we use mixed-precision: keep key/value caches in higher precision for critical spans. second, we run quality monitors and regression alerts tied to prompt sets — Redwood Optimize can flag shifts in hallucination rates after a quantization change.
[24:52] Tara: about caching prefix vs suffix — you recommend storing prefixes more aggressively?
[24:57] Priya: Prefixes typically have higher re-use across turns; suffixes often are ephemeral. So yes, keep prefix hot. But the selector helps decide exceptions.
[25:06] [30:00] Marco: For the benchmark plan, can you sketch the steps we'll do inside our VPC?
[30:06] Priya: Step 1: deploy private bundle to a small cluster (2 nodes) with dedicated EBS for cold store. Step 2: run deterministic baseline with async and batching off. Step 3: enable tiered KV + continuous batching but with conservative wait timers. Step 4: enable learned selector and async prefetch. Step 5: run production-like concurrency sweep and collect metrics. We'll provide the scripts for orchestration and metric collection.
[30:31] Elena: What's the expected run time for the full sweep?
[30:34] Omar: Depends on concurrency sweep but plan for 6-10 hours to get stable tails. We'll sample p99 across repeated runs.
[30:42] Marco: Are there any known bugs around 128k+ in the current runtime? we've seen some pointer bugs in other stacks.
[30:48] Priya: We had a couple of issues last quarter around KV offset wrapping on older runtimes; patched in 2026-02. If you run the latest private bundle we include those fixes. We'll include a small verification test in the harness.
[30:59] [44:00] Tara: question — what's the minimum GPU footprint to get reasonable p99 at 128k?
[44:05] Omar: For experimental workloads, 4x A100 is the minimum to get sub-1s p99 with optimized caching. For production headroom we recommend 8x A100 or equivalent with reserved capacity; that gives room for batching and concurrency. If you use quantized kernels on newer amps, you might get away with fewer cards but need to validate quality.
[44:26] Marco: And how do you measure cost per 1M tokens? is that from reserved capacity or host-level?
[44:31] Jamal: We give both: raw infra cost estimate and Redwood usage-based cost. For reserved capacity we amortize GPU + storage + ops over committed usage; the estimate will be in the pricing doc I'll share.
[44:45] [55:10] Elena: Let's talk about edge cases — e.g., multi-document references where the answer requires stitching across 200k tokens. Does nonlinear slicing risk dropping essential cross-document links?
[55:22] Priya: The selector is tuned to preserve cross-document references by promoting chunks that have high linking scores. We also maintain a lightweight graph of entities to bias retention. But there's always an application-level risk — that's why we recommend domain-specific evals.
[55:40] Marco: Could you do a quick live walkthrough of the harness config?
[55:45] Priya: Sure, switching to my screen... (screen share noise) The harness config has knobs: chunk_size_range, selector_threshold, prefetch_depth, batch_wait_ms, fallback_policy (none|deterministic|partial). Here you can see defaults we used in lab for 128k: chunk_size_range 64-2048 tokens, selector_threshold 0.42, prefetch_depth 3, batch_wait_ms 18ms.
[56:10] Tara: if we want lower latency at cost increase what's the recommended change?
[56:13] Priya: Lower batch_wait_ms to 8-10ms, reduce prefetch depth to 1, and increase tier0 pin fraction for prefixes. That increases infra cost but lowers p99.
[56:26] [67:12] Elena: OK, last bit — failure modes. If cold store SSD experiences IO spikes, what happens?
[67:18] Omar: We throttle cold fetches and fall back to a reduced attention window in extreme cases; there's also a circuit breaker to avoid cascading stalls. We'll surface alerts and automatically switch to a model variant with smaller memory if necessary.
[67:33] Marco: That adaptive fallback sounds useful. Is model fallback automated or operator triggered?
[67:37] Priya: Can be automated via policy: e.g., on >5% cold fetch latency spikes, route new requests to cheaper variant and continue async recovery. You can opt-in.
[67:48] Elena: Great. I think we have enough to start.
[67:52] Jamal: Recap of action items — Priya will share the harness and slicing doc, Marco will provide sample corpus and grant access, Omar will prepare an initial perf checklist, I'll share pricing and dedicated/private deployment options.
[68:05] Tara: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[68:10] Marco: thanks folks.
[68:14] Jamal: we'll follow up via email with links and calendar invites.
